summary: The note describes the 1939 German ultimatum to Lithuania, in which Joachim von Ribbentrop demanded that Lithuania cede the Klaipėda Region, threatening Wehrmacht invasion. Lithuania accepted on 22 March 1939, after the Nazi occupation of Czechoslovakia five days earlier and amid the appeasement policies of Britain and France. It was Germany's last territorial acquisition before World War II. The note also gives background on Klaipėda's status after World War I, the 1923 Klaipėda Revolt, and rising German-Lithuanian tensions in the 1930s.
one_line: Nazi Germany's March 1939 ultimatum forcing Lithuania to cede the Klaipėda Region, its last pre-war territorial gain.
key_facts: Joachim von Ribbentrop, Foreign Minister of Nazi Germany, presented an oral ultimatum to Juozas Urbšys, Foreign Minister of Lithuania, on 20 March 1939.
The ultimatum demanded that Lithuania give up the Klaipėda Region (also known as the Memel Territory), or the Wehrmacht would invade Lithuania.
The ultimatum was issued just five days after the Nazi occupation of Czechoslovakia.
The 1924 Klaipėda Convention guaranteed protection of the status quo in the region, but its four signatories did not offer any material assistance.
The United Kingdom and France followed a policy of appeasement, while Italy and Japan openly supported Germany.
Lithuania was forced to accept the ultimatum on 22 March 1939.
The ultimatum proved to be the last territorial acquisition for Germany before World War II.
Klaipėda (German: Memel) was detached from Germany by Article 28 of the Treaty of Versailles and was governed by the Allies according to Article 99.
Lithuania organized the Klaipėda Revolt in January 1923, with support from Soviet Russia and Germany.
The Klaipėda region covered about 2,400 km² and had a population of approximately 140,000.
Germany and Lithuania signed a border treaty in January 1928 that left Klaipėda on the Lithuanian side.
In February 1934, the Lithuanian government arrested dozens of pro-Nazi activists, prompting Germany to declare a boycott of Lithuanian agricultural imports.
The boycott caused an economic crisis in Suvalkija (southern Lithuania), where farmers organized violent protests.
After the plebiscite in Saar, most of the pro-Nazi prisoners received amnesty, which weakened Lithuanian prestige in Klaipėda and abroad.
The ultimatum produced a major downturn in Lithuania's economy and escalated pre-war tensions across Europe.
